title: Lou Gehrig
wiki_lead:
Henry Louis Gehrig ( GAIR-ig; born Heinrich Ludwig Gehrig; June 19, 1903 – June 2, 1941) was an American professional baseball first baseman who played 17 seasons in Major League Baseball (MLB) for the New York Yankees. Gehrig was renowned for his prowess as a hitter and for his durability, which earned him the nickname "the Iron Horse", and he is regarded as one of the greatest baseball players of all time. Gehrig was an All-Star seven consecutive times, a Triple Crown winner once, an American League (AL) Most Valuable Player twice and a member of six World Series champion teams. He had a career .340 batting average, .632 slugging average, and a .447 on-base average. He hit 493 home runs and had 1,995 runs batted in (RBIs). He is also one of 21 players to hit four home runs in a single game. In 1939, Gehrig was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame and was the first MLB player to have his uniform number retired by a team when his number 4 was retired by the Yankees.
A native of New York City and a student at Columbia University, Gehrig signed with the Yankees on April 29, 1923. He set several major-league records during his career, including the most career grand slams (23; since broken by Alex Rodriguez) and most consecutive games played (2,130), a record that stood for 56 years and was considered unbreakable until Cal Ripken Jr. surpassed it in 1995. Gehrig's consecutive game streak ended on May 2, 1939, when he voluntarily took himself out of the lineup, stunning both players and fans, after his performance in the field had become hampered by an undiagnosed ailment; it was subsequently confirmed to be amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), an incurable neuromuscular illness that since then is sometimes referred to as "Lou Gehrig's disease" in the United States.
Gehrig never played again and retired in 1939 at age 36. Two weeks later, the ball club held a Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day on July 4, 1939, at the close of which he delivered his speech declaring himself the "luckiest man on the face of the earth" at Yankee Stadium. Two years later, Gehrig died of complications from ALS. In 1969, the Baseball Writers' Association of America voted Gehrig the greatest first baseman of all time, and he was the leading vote-getter on the MLB All-Century Team, chosen by fans in 1999. A monument in Gehrig's honor, originally dedicated by the Yankees in 1941, prominently features in Monument Park at the new Yankee Stadium. The Lou Gehrig Memorial Award is given annually to the MLB player who best exhibits Gehrig's integrity and character.

Early life

grok_lead: Lou Gehrig, born Henry Louis Gehrig on June 19, 1903, in New York City, was an American professional baseball first baseman renowned for his extraordinary durability and power hitting during a 17-season career with the New York Yankees from 1923 to 1939. Often called the " Iron Horse," Gehrig set the major league record for consecutive games played at 2,130, a streak that stood until 1995 and symbolized his relentless work ethic. He amassed a.340 batting average, 493 home runs, and 1,995 runs batted in over his career, earning two American League Most Valuable Player Awards in 1927 and 1936, while helping the Yankees win seven pennants and six World Series titles. Diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) in 1939, the disease that later became known as Lou Gehrig's disease, he retired abruptly that year at age 35 and died on June 2, 1941, at age 37 in the Bronx, New York. Inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1939 via special election, Gehrig's legacy endures as one of baseball's greatest players and a symbol of courage in the face of adversity. Born to German immigrant parents Heinrich and Christina Gehrig in Manhattan's Yorkville neighborhood, Gehrig was an only surviving child after his siblings died in infancy, fostering a close-knit family dynamic that emphasized education and athletics. He excelled in baseball and football at Commerce High School, graduating in 1921, before attending Columbia University on a football scholarship, where he also starred in baseball and set a school record with a 400-foot home run in an exhibition game against the Yankees in 1923. Signed directly by the Yankees that spring without completing his degree, Gehrig made his major league debut on June 15, 1923, and quickly rose to prominence as Babe Ruth's teammate and successor in the lineup. Gehrig's career peaked in the late 1920s and 1930s, forming the famed "Murderers' Row" lineup with Ruth and later leading the team to dominance after Ruth's departure. In 1934, he won the Triple Crown with a.363 batting average, 49 home runs, and 166 RBIs, and he holds the American League single-season RBI record of 184 from 1931. Named the Yankees' captain in 1935, Gehrig played every inning of every game during his streak, which began on June 1, 1925, after Wally Pipp's injury, and ended only when his physical decline became undeniable. His consistency was unmatched, with 13 seasons producing at least 100 runs scored and 100 RBIs, and he retired holding or sharing numerous records, including 23 grand slams. By 1938, Gehrig's performance had mysteriously declined, prompting concern among teammates and fans; tests at the Mayo Clinic in June 1939 confirmed ALS, a progressive neurodegenerative disease with no known cure. On July 4, 1939, at Yankee Stadium, he delivered his iconic "Luckiest Man on the Face of the Earth" farewell speech to a tearful crowd of 62,000, encapsulating his humility and gratitude amid tragedy. Post-retirement, Gehrig served as a parole commissioner for New York City until his death, and his number 4 became the first retired in major league baseball history. Today, ALS awareness efforts and research continue to honor his name, while his statistical prowess and ironclad streak cement his status as a baseball immortal.
